title: SQL vs NoSQL & the CAP Theorem
tagline: Why there is no perfect distributed database — and how to pick the right store for your workload.

sections.content:
Every application you build rests on a storage layer, and the choice of that layer shapes almost every architectural decision that follows. For the first half-century of commercial computing, that choice was simple: you used a relational database, you learned SQL, and you trusted your data to tables and foreign keys. The relational model, invented by Edgar Codd at IBM in 1970, was so expressive and so rigorously grounded in mathematics that it dominated essentially everything.

Then came the internet at scale. Companies like Google, Amazon, and Facebook discovered that the guarantees relational databases provide — strict schemas, multi-table joins, serializable transactions — come at a cost: **they are hard to distribute**. Partitioning a relational database across many machines while preserving all its correctness guarantees requires extraordinary coordination. At the scale of billions of users and petabytes of data, that coordination cost becomes prohibitive.

Out of this pressure emerged an entire ecosystem of alternative data stores, loosely grouped under the label **NoSQL** (which originally stood for 'Non SQL' and was later re-interpreted as 'Not Only SQL'). These systems traded away some of SQL's guarantees in exchange for horizontal scalability, flexible schemas, and access patterns tuned to specific workloads. Document stores, key-value caches, wide-column engines, graph databases — each family makes a different set of trade-offs.

In 2000, Eric Brewer proposed the **CAP theorem** as a formal framework for understanding what distributed databases can and cannot promise. Proved rigorously by Gilbert and Lynch in 2002, it states that during a network partition — when nodes in a cluster cannot communicate — a distributed system must choose between two properties: **Consistency** (every read reflects the latest write) or **Availability** (every request receives a response, even if the data may be stale). This is not an engineering failure; it is a mathematical impossibility to have both simultaneously.

In this chapter we will build a complete mental model: what SQL gives you and why, what the NoSQL families are and when each shines, how the CAP theorem works mechanically, how sharding and replication scale data horizontally, and how to make the right choice for a given workload. These are some of the most common senior engineering interview topics, and mastering them is a prerequisite for any serious system design conversation.

sections.title: The Split-Brain Filing Room
sections.content:
Imagine a large company with two filing rooms on opposite sides of a building, both maintaining identical copies of the employee records. A courier runs between them all day to keep the copies in sync. Now imagine the courier's hallway is blocked — a network partition.

The filing-room managers now face a choice. They can **stop accepting updates** until the hallway reopens (that is Consistency: readers are guaranteed to see the latest data, but no writes can proceed). Or they can **keep accepting updates independently**, knowing the copies will drift apart and will need to be reconciled later when the hallway reopens (that is Availability: the service stays up, but readers might see stale records).

A single filing room with no courier to worry about can offer both guarantees simultaneously — that is why a standalone PostgreSQL instance is sometimes described as 'CA', even though partition tolerance is moot when there is nothing to partition. In a real distributed system, the hallway is the network, and it will be blocked eventually. The partition is not hypothetical — it is a certainty at scale. The question is only what you sacrifice when it happens.

sections.title: Relational Databases: The SQL Fortress
sections.content:
A **relational database** organises data into **tables** (also called relations in the mathematical sense). Each table has a fixed **schema** — a list of named, typed columns. Rows are individual records. Relationships between entities are expressed via **foreign keys**: a column in one table holding the primary key value of a row in another table.

SQL (Structured Query Language) is the interface. It is **declarative**: you describe *what* you want, not *how* to retrieve it. The database's query optimizer — a sophisticated piece of software — reads your SQL, consults statistics about table sizes and index coverage, and generates an efficient **execution plan**. This separation of intent from execution is enormously powerful. A query that takes ten lines of SQL might be rewritten by the optimizer into a plan that uses a hash join plus a bitmap index scan, executing in milliseconds against a table with a hundred million rows.

The correctness guarantees SQL databases offer are called **ACID**:
- **Atomicity**: a transaction either commits entirely or rolls back entirely — no partial writes.
- **Consistency**: every transaction brings the database from one valid state to another — constraints (foreign keys, CHECK clauses, UNIQUE indexes) are always enforced.
- **Isolation**: concurrent transactions do not see each other's intermediate states — the database appears to execute them serially.
- **Durability**: once committed, a transaction survives crashes — the write-ahead log (WAL) ensures recovery.

These four properties are what make relational databases the default choice for financial systems, ERP/CRM, healthcare records, and any domain where incorrect data has legal, safety, or monetary consequences. When the correctness contract must be ironclad, SQL is the answer.

The trade-off is **scaling writes**. SQL's ACID guarantees require coordination: locks, two-phase commit for distributed transactions, WAL flushing to disk. On a single powerful server this coordination is cheap. Spread it across dozens of nodes and the coordination overhead dominates. This is why SQL databases historically scaled **vertically** (bigger machines) while NoSQL systems are designed to scale **horizontally** (more machines).

PostgreSQL, MySQL/MariaDB, and SQLite are the dominant open-source relational databases. In the cloud, Amazon Aurora, Google Cloud Spanner, and Azure SQL Database add distribution on top of the SQL model — though always at the cost of some guarantee weakening or latency increase.

sections.title: The Four NoSQL Families — and When to Reach for Each
sections.content:
**NoSQL** is not a single technology but an umbrella for several distinct storage paradigms, each optimised for a different shape of data and access pattern. Confusing them is the most common mistake engineers make when evaluating databases.

**Document stores** (MongoDB, Firestore, CouchDB) store semi-structured, JSON-like documents. Each document is a self-contained blob of nested fields and arrays — there is no join required to load a complete entity because all its attributes live in one place. This is called **denormalisation by default**. Document stores excel when the shape of data varies between records (user profiles with different optional fields), when you often load an entire entity at once, and when your team iterates rapidly on the schema. The downside: querying across multiple document collections is expensive (`$lookup` in MongoDB is far slower than a SQL join) and you must manage data consistency manually — if a user's email appears in multiple documents, you must update them all.

**Key-value stores** (Redis, DynamoDB, Memcached) are the simplest possible abstraction: a giant hash map. Given a key, retrieve the value — always O(1), always lightning fast. Redis keeps everything in memory with optional persistence to disk; lookups are measured in microseconds. Key-value stores are the natural fit for sessions, caches, feature flags, rate-limiting counters, and leaderboards. Their limitation is the absence of structure: you cannot query by anything other than the key, and complex relationships are invisible to the database.

**Wide-column stores** (Apache Cassandra, HBase, ScyllaDB) are more nuanced. Despite their name they are closer to a distributed sorted map than to a traditional column store. Data is organised by a **partition key** (which shard holds this row), a **clustering key** (the sort order within a partition), and an arbitrary set of columns that can vary per row. Cassandra is engineered for **write-heavy, append-intensive** workloads: time-series data, IoT sensor readings, event logs, and analytics at scale. It achieves extraordinary write throughput by writing to an in-memory structure first (the memtable), flushing to disk sequentially (SSTables), and never performing in-place updates — instead, newer writes simply shadow older ones. The trade-off is that the data model must be designed **query-first**: you define your tables around the queries you will run, not around the relationships between entities.

**Graph databases** (Neo4j, Amazon Neptune, ArangoDB) represent data as **nodes** and **edges** — vertices and relationships in graph theory terms. Both nodes and edges can carry properties. The key advantage is **native relationship traversal**: finding 'all friends of friends within 3 hops who live in Berlin' is an O(edges traversed) operation in a graph database versus an O(table-size) multi-join in SQL. Social networks, recommendation engines, fraud detection (spotting suspicious transaction chains), and knowledge graphs are the canonical use cases. Graph databases shine when relationships are the query, not the afterthought.

sections.label: Example
sections.code:
-- ── SQL: expressive declarative query with JOINs ──────────────
-- 'Top 10 customers by order count in the last 30 days'
SELECT
  u.id,
  u.name,
  u.email,
  COUNT(o.id)          AS order_count,
  SUM(o.total_amount)  AS total_spent
FROM users u
JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id
WHERE o.created_at >= NOW() - INTERVAL '30 days'
  AND o.status = 'completed'
GROUP BY u.id, u.name, u.email
HAVING COUNT(o.id) > 5
ORDER BY order_count DESC
LIMIT 10;

-- The optimizer may choose:
--   1. Index scan on orders.created_at
--   2. Hash join with users on user_id
--   3. Hash aggregate for GROUP BY
-- You describe WHAT; the optimizer decides HOW.

-- ── MongoDB equivalent (aggregation pipeline) ─────────────────
-- db.orders.aggregate([
--   { $match: { created_at: { $gte: thirtyDaysAgo },
--               status: 'completed' } },
--   { $group: { _id: '$user_id',
--               order_count: { $sum: 1 },
--               total_spent: { $sum: '$total_amount' } } },
--   { $match: { order_count: { $gt: 5 } } },
--   // $lookup = cross-collection join (expensive, sequential)
--   { $lookup: { from: 'users', localField: '_id',
--                foreignField: '_id', as: 'user' } },
--   { $unwind: '$user' },
--   { $sort: { order_count: -1 } },
--   { $limit: 10 }
-- ])
sections.explanation: The SQL version is 14 lines and lets the optimizer pick the best execution plan. The MongoDB version is longer, requires a $lookup (which performs a sequential collection scan per matched group by default unless carefully indexed), and has far fewer optimizer options. For ad-hoc analytical queries across multiple entities, SQL is almost always the right choice. MongoDB wins when you load whole documents by _id without joins.

sections.title: The CAP Theorem — What It Actually Says
sections.content:
The **CAP theorem** states that a distributed data store can guarantee at most two of the following three properties simultaneously:

- **Consistency (C)**: Every read receives the most recent write or an error. All nodes see the same data at the same time. This is **linearizability** in formal terms — every operation appears to happen instantaneously at some point between its start and end.
- **Availability (A)**: Every request receives a response — success or failure — without guarantee that it contains the most recent data. The system never returns an error because it cannot reach the latest state.
- **Partition Tolerance (P)**: The system continues to operate even when an arbitrary number of messages between nodes are dropped or delayed — a network partition.

Here is the critical nuance that most explanations miss: **in any real distributed system, partition tolerance is non-negotiable**. Network partitions happen. Cables are cut, switches fail, cloud availability zones lose connectivity. A system that abandons partition tolerance when a partition occurs is simply offline — which violates availability anyway. So the real choice is not 'pick two of three'; it is:

> **When a partition happens, do you prioritise Consistency (return an error rather than stale data) or Availability (return possibly-stale data rather than an error)?**

This is the **CP vs AP** choice. 'CA' systems are really just single-node systems where partitions are not relevant.

**CP systems** (Consistency + Partition Tolerance): HBase, Zookeeper, etcd, MongoDB with majority write concern. During a partition, a CP system refuses to serve requests that cannot be guaranteed to reflect the latest state. You might get an error: 'Cannot reach quorum'. Banks, inventory systems, and leader-election services want CP — it is worse to show a customer a balance that is $1000 too high than to show them a temporary error.

**AP systems** (Availability + Partition Tolerance): Cassandra, DynamoDB, CouchDB, Riak. During a partition, AP systems continue to serve requests from whichever nodes are reachable, potentially returning stale data. When the partition heals, the system reconciles diverged writes — **eventual consistency**. Social feeds, shopping carts, DNS, and analytics counters accept eventual consistency — showing a user a post that is two seconds old is not a business problem.

sections.title: Eventual Consistency — Mechanics and Consequences
sections.content:
**Eventual consistency** is the consistency model adopted by AP systems. It is a weaker guarantee than linearizability: if no new writes are made to a key, eventually all replicas will converge to the same value. During the period before convergence, different clients reading from different replicas may see different values for the same key.

In Cassandra, writes use a concept called **quorum**. If you have a replication factor of 3 (each row is stored on three nodes) and you configure writes to succeed when 2 out of 3 nodes acknowledge (`QUORUM`), and reads to also require acknowledgment from 2 out of 3 nodes, then `R + W > N` (2 + 2 > 3) — you are guaranteed to always read at least one node that has the latest write. This is called a **quorum read/write** and provides strong consistency despite an AP foundation. Lowering to `ONE` (only one node must acknowledge) maximises throughput and availability but allows reads of stale data.

This tunability is a key insight: most modern distributed databases do not sit strictly at one point on the CAP spectrum — they let operators **tune the trade-off per operation**.

**Conflict resolution** becomes necessary when diverged writes must be merged. Common strategies:
- **Last-Write-Wins (LWW)**: the write with the highest timestamp wins. Simple but loses data in concurrent scenarios.
- **Version vectors / vector clocks**: each replica maintains a vector of write counts per node. Causally related updates can be ordered; concurrent updates are flagged for application-level resolution.
- **CRDTs (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types)**: data structures designed so that any merge of concurrent updates is commutative, associative, and idempotent — counters, sets, and registers can be made CRDT-safe.

Riak and some Redis Cluster configurations use CRDTs. DynamoDB lets application code define reconciliation logic. Cassandra defaults to LWW.

sequenceDiagram

  participant N2 as "Node B"
  participant C2 as "Client 2"
  C1->>N1: "Write x=5"
  Note over N1,N2: "Network partition"
  C2->>N2: "Write x=7"

sections.caption: During a partition, two nodes accept concurrent writes. When the partition heals, Last-Write-Wins (LWW) picks the higher timestamp, silently discarding Client 1's write. This data loss is the price of availability.

sections.title: Sharding: Scaling Writes Horizontally
sections.content:
**Sharding** (also called horizontal partitioning) is the technique of splitting a dataset across multiple database nodes, each responsible for a disjoint subset of the data. Each node — called a **shard** — is a fully independent database server. No single machine holds all the data.

Sharding solves the write bottleneck: instead of one node absorbing all writes, each shard absorbs writes for its partition only. With 10 shards of equal size, write throughput scales roughly linearly (minus coordination overhead).

**How data is routed to a shard** is determined by the **shard key** and the **partitioning strategy**:

- **Hash partitioning**: compute `hash(shard_key) mod N` where N is the number of shards. Data is evenly distributed and lookups are O(1). The downside: range queries require hitting every shard (a scatter-gather fan-out). This is how Cassandra and Redis Cluster work by default.
- **Range partitioning**: assign ranges of the shard key to specific shards (e.g., users A–M on shard 1, N–Z on shard 2). Range queries are efficient — only the relevant shards are queried. The risk is **hot spots**: if the range partition is on a monotonically increasing value (like a timestamp or auto-increment ID), all new writes always land on the last shard.
- **Directory-based partitioning**: a lookup table maps each key to its shard. Maximum flexibility; the risk is that the lookup table becomes a single point of failure and a bottleneck.

**Choosing the shard key** is one of the most consequential decisions in database design. A good shard key has:
1. **High cardinality**: enough distinct values to spread data evenly across shards.
2. **Uniform distribution**: not skewed so that 80% of writes go to one value.
3. **Query alignment**: the most common queries filter by the shard key — otherwise every query fans out to all shards.
4. **Immutability**: if the shard key value changes, the row must be moved to a different shard — an expensive operation.

**Cross-shard operations** are the main cost of sharding. A query that joins data from multiple shards must be routed to each relevant shard, the results collected (**scatter**) and merged at a coordinator node (**gather**). Distributed transactions across shards require two-phase commit (2PC) — expensive and error-prone. Most sharded systems avoid cross-shard joins by denormalising data so that everything needed for a query lives on the same shard.

flowchart LR

  RT -->|"hash(user_id) mod 3 = 0"| S0["Shard 0\nusers 0..33%"]
  RT -->|"hash(user_id) mod 3 = 1"| S1["Shard 1\nusers 33..66%"]
  RT -->|"hash(user_id) mod 3 = 2"| S2["Shard 2\nusers 66..100%"]

sections.caption: Sharding distributes writes across three shards via hash partitioning. Each shard is replicated for read scale and fault tolerance. The router holds the mapping logic.

sections.title: Replication: Scaling Reads and Surviving Failures
sections.content:
**Replication** is the practice of maintaining multiple identical (or near-identical) copies of the same data on different nodes. Unlike sharding — which splits the data — replication duplicates it. The two techniques compose: most large-scale systems shard for write capacity and replicate each shard for read capacity and fault tolerance.

**Primary-replica replication** (also called master-slave) is the classic model. One node — the **primary** — accepts all writes. It records each write to a replication log (the WAL in PostgreSQL, the binlog in MySQL). Replica nodes tail this log and apply the same writes in order, staying in sync with the primary. Reads can be served from any replica, multiplying read throughput by the number of replicas. If the primary fails, a replica is promoted — a process called **failover**.

The danger in primary-replica replication is **replication lag**: replicas apply writes asynchronously, so for a brief window after a write, reading from a replica may return stale data. This is the classic 'read-your-own-writes' consistency problem: a user writes a post and immediately reads their feed — if the read hits a replica that has not caught up, the post appears to be missing.

Mitigation strategies:
- **Read-your-own-writes**: route reads for a user to the primary for a short window after that user's write.
- **Monotonic reads**: ensure a user always reads from the same replica during a session — preventing them from seeing data going 'backwards'.
- **Synchronous replication**: the primary waits for at least one replica to confirm the write before returning success. Eliminates lag but adds write latency.

**Multi-primary replication** (active-active) allows writes on multiple nodes simultaneously. Conflict resolution (as discussed under eventual consistency) becomes necessary. This is how CouchDB and some DynamoDB Global Tables configurations work.

**Leaderless replication** (used by Cassandra and Riak) has no designated primary. Any node can accept a write. The client writes to N nodes using quorum rules to determine success. This eliminates the single-write-path bottleneck and the failover delay, at the cost of requiring quorum-based conflict resolution.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: Hash-based shard routing distributes keys deterministically — given the same key and shard count, you always get the same shard. The quorum formula R + W > N is the mathematical guarantee of strong consistency in a leaderless replication system: because the read set and write set must overlap, at least one node in any read quorum holds the latest write.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: This decision tree encodes the core logic of database selection: ACID first, then access pattern, then write scale. In real system design interviews, walking through this tree systematically demonstrates architectural maturity. The key insight is that the access pattern drives the schema design, not the other way around.

sections.content: **PACELC — the extension to CAP**: In 2012, Daniel Abadi proposed PACELC to address a gap in CAP: even when there is *no* partition, distributed systems face a trade-off between **Latency** and **Consistency**. A fully synchronous replication scheme gives strong consistency but adds write latency (must wait for remote acknowledgment). PACELC says: when Partitioned, choose between A and C; Else (when running normally), choose between L and C. Cassandra is PA/EL (prefers availability during partition, prefers low latency otherwise). PostgreSQL (single-node) is PC/EC. This is a more complete model for evaluating real systems.

**Common interview traps and misconceptions to master:**

'Pick two of three in CAP' is misleading — P is mandatory. The real choice is CP vs AP during a partition.

MongoDB is not automatically AP — with majority write and read concern it behaves as CP. Weaker settings push it toward AP. Always clarify the concern level.

A **hot shard** is the most common scaling failure in sharded systems. If you choose a monotonically increasing shard key (auto-increment ID, timestamp), 100% of new writes go to one shard. Always hash or composite-key to spread load.

'Eventual consistency' does not mean 'frequently inconsistent'. Under low load with fast networks, replicas may be within milliseconds of each other. Eventual consistency is only observable under concurrent conflicting writes — which may be rare for your workload.

SQL and NoSQL are not mutually exclusive. Most production architectures use both: PostgreSQL for transactional data, Redis for caching, and Cassandra or DynamoDB for high-volume event streams. Polyglot persistence is the norm at scale.

items: **SQL databases** offer ACID transactions, expressive JOINs, and a query optimizer — the right default for financial, ERP, and relational workloads where correctness is non-negotiable.

**NoSQL families each optimise for a specific access pattern**: document stores for flexible hierarchical data, key-value for O(1) point lookups, wide-column for append-heavy time-series at scale, graph for multi-hop relationship traversal.

**CAP theorem**: during a network partition, a distributed system must choose Consistency (return error, never stale) or Availability (respond, possibly stale). Partition tolerance is mandatory in any real distributed system — 'CA' only applies to single-node systems.
**Eventual consistency** means replicas converge after a partition heals. Quorum rules (R + W > N) let operators tune where on the CP/AP spectrum a system sits on a per-operation basis.

**Sharding** partitions data across nodes for write scale. The shard key must have high cardinality, uniform distribution, and align with the most common query patterns. Avoid monotonically-increasing shard keys to prevent hot shards.

**Replication** duplicates data across nodes for read scale and fault tolerance. Primary-replica replication introduces replication lag — the read-your-own-writes problem must be addressed in application design.

**Polyglot persistence** is the norm at scale: use PostgreSQL for transactions, Redis for caching, Cassandra for event streams, and Neo4j for graph queries — picking each tool for the access pattern it was designed for.

quiz.question: According to the CAP theorem, why is 'Partition Tolerance' non-negotiable in any real distributed system?
options: Network partitions are mathematically impossible to prevent, so any system that abandons P is simply unavailable when splits occur
Partition tolerance is optional — small clusters can be configured to avoid it
Abandoning partition tolerance improves both consistency and availability simultaneously
Partition tolerance only applies to systems with more than 100 nodes
quiz.explanation: Network partitions — nodes losing the ability to communicate — happen in all real distributed systems due to hardware failures, software bugs, and network outages. A system that abandons P when a partition happens is simply down. So the real choice during a partition is Consistency vs Availability, not which two of three properties to pick.

quiz.question: A banking system must never show an incorrect account balance. It should return an error rather than stale data during a network partition. Which CAP profile should it adopt?
options: AP — prioritise availability so customers can always check balances
CP — prioritise consistency, returning an error during a partition rather than stale data
CA — use a system with no partition tolerance
ACID — relational databases are immune to CAP
quiz.explanation: A CP system refuses requests that cannot be guaranteed to reflect the latest state during a partition. For a bank, showing an incorrect balance (stale data) could allow overdrafts or double-spends — an error message is safer. HBase and Zookeeper are CP; so is MongoDB with majority write concern.

quiz.question: In Cassandra with replication factor N=3, what is the minimum combined read quorum (R) and write quorum (W) that guarantees strong consistency?
options: R=1, W=1 (total 2) — fast and consistent
R=2, W=2 (total 4) — because R + W > N ensures overlap
R=3, W=3 (total 6) — all replicas must agree
R=1, W=3 (total 4) — writing to all ensures reads are always fresh
quiz.explanation: The quorum condition for strong consistency is R + W > N. With N=3, R=2 and W=2 gives 4 > 3, which guarantees the read set and write set overlap by at least one node — that node holds the latest write. R=1,W=1 gives 2 which is not greater than 3, allowing stale reads.

quiz.question: A team chooses a timestamp column as the shard key for a high-traffic event table. What failure mode will they experience?
options: Hash collisions will corrupt data across shards
Range queries will become impossible because timestamps are too granular
All new writes will land on the latest-timestamp shard, creating a hot spot while other shards sit idle
Replication lag will increase because timestamps change frequently
quiz.explanation: A monotonically increasing shard key (timestamp, auto-increment ID) means the 'current' shard always receives 100% of new writes. This defeats horizontal scaling — one shard is overwhelmed while others are underutilised. The fix is to hash the key or use a composite key that distributes writes evenly.

quiz.question: Which NoSQL family is architecturally best suited for the query 'find all accounts that transacted with account X within two degrees of separation'?
options: Wide-column store — optimised for time-ordered lookups
Document store — nested documents can hold transaction lists
Key-value store — O(1) lookups for each account ID
Graph database — native multi-hop edge traversal is O(edges), not O(table size)
quiz.explanation: Graph databases store relationships as first-class citizens (edges with properties). A two-hop traversal ('accounts that transacted with accounts that transacted with X') is O(edges followed), which is far more efficient than performing multiple expensive SQL JOINs. This is exactly the fraud detection use case that drives graph database adoption in financial services.

quiz.question: What is the primary advantage of the SQL query optimizer over MongoDB's aggregation pipeline for ad-hoc analytical queries?
options: SQL always runs faster because it is compiled to native code
The SQL optimizer can choose among multiple join algorithms (hash join, merge join, index nested-loop) based on statistics; the aggregation pipeline is a fixed procedural sequence
SQL queries can be cached by the browser; MongoDB queries cannot
SQL supports more data types than MongoDB's BSON format
quiz.explanation: SQL is declarative — you describe what to retrieve and the optimizer generates a plan. It can choose hash joins, merge joins, or nested-loop joins based on table cardinality and index coverage. MongoDB's aggregation pipeline is procedural: stages execute in the order written, with far fewer optimizer choices. For complex multi-collection queries, SQL's optimizer advantage is decisive.

quiz.question: A social media application must always return a user's feed, even if slightly stale, to maximise uptime during network issues. Which database and consistency model fits best?
options: PostgreSQL with serializable isolation — ACID guarantees freshness
HBase with strong consistency — CP systems are reliable
Cassandra with ONE consistency level — AP, eventual consistency, always available
Redis in standalone mode — fastest in-memory reads
quiz.explanation: Social feeds tolerate stale data — showing a post two seconds late is not a business problem. Cassandra with consistency level ONE (write/read acknowledged by a single node) maximises availability at the cost of possible staleness. This is the archetypal AP use case. HBase/CP would error during a partition, hurting availability — the wrong trade-off for a social feed.

quiz.question: What does 'replication lag' mean in a primary-replica setup, and which application pattern does it most directly break?
options: The delay in applying schema migrations across all replicas — breaks deployment automation
The window during which a replica has not yet applied the primary's latest writes — breaks read-your-own-writes consistency
The time difference between UTC and local time in replica timestamps — breaks date-range queries
Network latency when routing cross-shard queries — breaks distributed JOINs
quiz.explanation: Replication lag is the asynchronous delay between a write landing on the primary and that write being replicated to and applied by replicas. If a user writes data and immediately reads from a replica that has not caught up, they see their own write missing — the read-your-own-writes consistency violation. Mitigations include routing reads to the primary briefly after a user's write, or using synchronous replication.

quiz.question: Which of the following is the best shard key for a global user table with 500 million users, where the most common query is 'look up a user by ID'?
options: created_at timestamp — enables chronological range queries
country_code — groups users by geography for locality
hash(user_id) — high cardinality, even distribution, aligns with point-lookup query pattern
last_login_at — distributes active users evenly across shards
quiz.explanation: hash(user_id) satisfies all good shard key criteria: high cardinality (500M distinct values), even distribution (a good hash function is uniform), and alignment with the primary access pattern (look up by user_id). Timestamp keys cause hot shards. Country codes have low cardinality — a shard for 'US' would hold 30%+ of all users. last_login_at changes frequently, making the key effectively mutable.

quiz.question: What does the PACELC model add to CAP that CAP does not address?
options: It adds a fourth property — Elasticity — measuring how quickly a system scales under load
It recognises that even without a partition, systems must trade off between Latency and Consistency in normal operation
It replaces Partition Tolerance with a probabilistic metric for network reliability
It extends CAP to cover storage durability and replication factor decisions
quiz.explanation: CAP only describes behaviour during a partition. PACELC (proposed by Abadi, 2012) adds the Else clause: when the system is running normally (no partition), it still must choose between lower Latency (respond before all replicas confirm) and stronger Consistency (wait for quorum before responding). Cassandra is PA/EL (availability during partition, low latency otherwise); a synchronous single-node PostgreSQL is effectively PC/EC.
